leaderPrimer:
Familiarity is the main obstacle in this study. Your group has heard the Sermon on the Mount all their lives: turn the other cheek, the lilies of the field, the house on the rock. The words have been worn smooth, and they slide past the conscience. Nobody in your room disagrees with this sermon, and that's the problem. Agreeing with it has become a polite way of ignoring it.

So your first job is to make the words strange again. Read them slowly, as if a teacher on a hillside were saying them for the first time to people who'd never heard anyone talk this way, because he was. Anger is the root of murder. A look can be adultery. Enemies are to be loved. Let the room feel how unreasonable it sounds before anyone rushes to manage it. You'll meet two ways out, and you'll want to close both: the one that files these commands under "ideals for another world," and the one that turns them into a ladder we climb by trying harder. The first produces comfortable disciples and the second produces exhausted ones.

Be especially careful in session three. The love of enemies can turn political in a few sentences, and it can wound someone who has been told to forgive an abuser and stay. Say clearly what the guide says: Jesus forbids revenge, not safety, justice or getting out. Keep the help information for this guide where you can reach it.

Bonhoeffer is a steady companion through the study. He wrote on this sermon in the 1930s and was hanged by the Nazi regime in April 1945. Quote him where the guide does, and don't make him say more than he said.

Lead as someone this sermon convicts. If you exempt yourself from the anger called principle or the money called stewardship, the room will nod for six weeks and change nothing. And keep the Preacher in view behind the preaching. Only one man ever built entirely on this rock, and he did it on the way to a cross for the rest of us. Let the sermon wound, then point to him, in that order, every week.

faq.q: Is the Sermon on the Mount even possible to keep, or is it an impossible ideal?
faq.a: This study refuses both easy answers. It isn't just an impossible ideal meant only to crush us, because Jesus plainly expects his hearers to do what he says, and he ends with a builder who hears and does. And it isn't a code we keep by trying harder, because the first beatitude blesses the poor in spirit, the people with nothing to bring. The sermon describes the life of someone who has surrendered to the King: given to empty hands, and then lived out by his power rather than ours. You don't keep it by gritting your teeth, and you aren't excused from it because it's hard.

faq.q: Does this study turn the gospel into a list of rules?
faq.a: No. Every session rests on the first beatitude, that the kingdom belongs to the poor in spirit, so the sermon is grace before it is demand. The study takes seriously the worry that Jesus' demands become a new legalism, and answers that doing is the fruit of living faith, not the root of salvation. It also warns against the opposite mistake, the cheap grace that makes obedience optional. Holding grace and demand together is harder than either, and it's what the sermon asks.

faq.q: Why does the study draw so much on Bonhoeffer?
faq.a: Because he read this sermon as a call to follow and not merely to admire, and he did it at great cost. The Cost of Discipleship (1937) was written while much of the German church was making its peace with the Nazi regime. His distinction between cheap grace and costly grace is a sharp tool for examining our own discipleship, and his line that "only he who believes is obedient, and only he who is obedient believes" holds together what the sermon won't let us split. He was hanged in April 1945, weeks before the war in Europe ended. The study quotes him only where his words can be checked.

faq.q: When Jesus says "judge not," does that mean Christians should never call anything wrong?
faq.a: No. A few verses later, in the same chapter, Jesus tells the same people to beware of false prophets and to know them by their fruit (Matthew 7:15-20). That takes moral discernment. What he forbids is the hypocrite's judgment, the man with a log in his own eye inspecting the speck in his brother's. And he doesn't say leave the speck alone. He says take out the log first, so you can see clearly enough to help. The verse requires humility before discernment, not the end of it.

faq.q: Does loving your enemies mean someone who is being abused has to stay?
faq.a: No. This command has been used to keep wounded people in harm's way, and that's a sin the church has to own. Loving an enemy means refusing personal revenge and wanting the other person's good. It never forbids getting to safety, seeking protection or going to the authorities. Someone leaving an abuser isn't breaking this command. Sometimes the most loving thing toward an abuser is to have him stopped. The command takes away the right to revenge, not the right to be safe. If this is your situation, please use the help information that comes with this guide.

faq.q: Is the study saying I shouldn't save money or plan for the future?
faq.a: No. Scripture praises the ant that stores up food (Proverbs 6:6-8) and says those who don't provide for their households have denied the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). Jesus isn't naming an amount; he's naming a master. Money becomes a god when we trust it to do what only God can do: keep us safe, prove our worth, guarantee tomorrow. You can save and plan while your security rests in God and you hold money with an open hand.

faq.q: The narrow gate sounds harsh. Why would a loving God make the way hard?
faq.a: The study doesn't soften the words, because Jesus does say the gate is narrow and few find it. But what makes it narrow isn't God being stingy with life. The way is Jesus himself, and there's no wider entrance we get to invent. The wide road lets you carry everything through: your self-rule, your idols, your refusal to change. The narrow gate is narrow because those don't fit. And the One who describes the gate is the One who came to stand in it and call everyone on the broad road to come this way.

faq.q: What if I've heard all this before and nothing in my life changes?
faq.a: Then the final session is about you, and about most of us. Jesus ends with two builders who heard the same words, and the only difference between the house that stood and the house that fell was doing. That's why every session ends with a concrete practice, and why the last one asks you to take the most convicting thing you've heard and do it that week.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Isn't the Sermon on the Mount impossible moralizing that makes people feel guilty?
faq.a: It's a fair suspicion. But notice how the sermon begins: by blessing people who have nothing to bring, which is the opposite of moralizing. The study takes seriously how impossible the demands sound, and it locates the power for any of them not in willpower but in a grace received first. The sermon isn't finally a list of demands. It's the description of a kingdom and an invitation from the King who preached it and then lived it all the way to a cross. You're free to weigh that. The study doesn't ask you to manufacture guilt or goodness. It asks you to consider the King.

faq.q: Why does the study keep turning the sermon on the writer and the leader?
faq.a: Because a study that pointed only at other people's sin would let everyone admire the sermon and do none of it, which is the house on the sand. The writer doesn't stand on the mountain looking down, and the study asks the leader not to either. A leader who can say "this convicts me too" can teach without contempt, as a fellow builder rather than a judge.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I haven't figured out the Sermon on the Mount myself?
faq.a: You don't need to have figured it out. You need to be truthful that you haven't. Every question comes with a note, and every session ends in prayer and a practice, so you aren't improvising. Your own admission of where this sermon convicts you may be the most pastoral thing in the room. Do refuse two failures: crushing the perfectionist and comforting the complacent. Protect the wounded, especially in session three. Read the leader's primer and let the sermon find you.

faq.q: Does the study promise that if I obey, my life will go well?
faq.a: No. The sermon ends with a storm that hits both houses, the wise builder's and the foolish one's. Obedience doesn't buy an easy life. What's promised is a foundation that holds, and that foundation is Christ himself. The point isn't the absence of the storm. It's what the storm shows you were standing on.

timeline.event: Moses receives the law at Sinai. Matthew sets Jesus on a mountain to teach, presenting him as one greater than Moses who fulfills the law rather than abolishing it.
Jesus teaches what Matthew records in chapters 5 to 7, opening with the Beatitudes and closing with the two builders. Luke gives a shorter, related sermon in Luke 6.
James, the brother of Jesus, writes that faith without works is dead and that we must be doers of the word and not hearers only, the warning of the two houses.
Matthew's Gospel gathers the teaching into chapters 5 to 7, framing Jesus as the new lawgiver on the mountain. Some scholars date the Gospel earlier.
Under intermittent persecution, many Christian writers take the love of enemies and the refusal to retaliate with great seriousness, and several urge believers not to take up the sword.
Augustine writes Our Lord's Sermon on the Mount, one of the earliest sustained commentaries, reading it as the pattern of the Christian life.
The first Anabaptists take the sermon as a literal rule of life. The Schleitheim Confession (1527) rejects oaths and the sword for believers, and many suffer severe persecution.
Martin Luther preaches on Matthew 5 to 7, insisting the sermon is for all Christians and must be held together with the gospel rather than turned into a way of earning salvation.
Dietrich Bonhoeffer publishes The Cost of Discipleship, built on his teaching of the sermon, and sets cheap grace against costly grace.
Bonhoeffer is hanged at Flossenbürg by the Nazi regime he had resisted, weeks before the war in Europe ended.
Martyn Lloyd-Jones publishes Studies in the Sermon on the Mount in two volumes, insisting it describes every Christian and isn't an ideal for a few.
John Stott publishes Christian Counter-Culture, later titled The Message of the Sermon on the Mount, presenting the sermon as the life of a community whose values run against the world's.
Dallas Willard publishes The Divine Conspiracy, reading the sermon as practical training for life in the kingdom now.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thanks for being here. The Sermon on the Mount is admired by nearly everyone and obeyed by very few, and over these weeks we're going to stop admiring it from a distance. Three things before we start. First, you can tell the truth here: about anger you've held onto, money you can't let go of, someone you can't forgive. Nobody will lecture you. Second, this study holds two things together. The sermon is grace first, given to people with empty hands, and then it asks for everything. We won't make it an ideal we're excused from, and we won't make it rules we keep by trying harder. Third, this sermon convicts me too. I'm not standing on the mountain looking down. Tonight we're looking at this together: ________. Let me read our passage, and then we'll sit with it for a moment before anyone says anything.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what Jesus says. Now let's bring it into the week we're about to walk into, because this sermon ends on exactly that question: whether what we've heard becomes something we do.
facilitatorScript.close: We'll stop there, even though it isn't all settled, because Jesus ended his sermon with a storm and a question, not a neat bow. Try the practice this week. Do the one thing you most clearly heard and haven't done. Spend some time with the reflection questions. The point was never to admire the sermon. It was to build on the rock. Let me pray for us before we go.

cadences.name: The full study (9 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, agree on confidentiality, and say plainly that the sermon is grace before it is demand. Walk slowly through session 1's opening question.
Week 2: Session 1, The Upside-Down Kingdom, full discussion and practice on the Beatitudes.
Week 3: Session 2, Salt, Light, and the Deeper Law, with extended time on the interior law reaching anger and lust.
Week 4: Session 3, Love Your Enemies, part one: revenge and turning the cheek, with careful time for anyone who has been hurt, and the help information within reach.
Week 5: Session 3 continued, the love of enemies grounded in the Father and the cross, plus practice on praying for an enemy.
Week 6: Session 4, Where Your Treasure Is, the two masters and the worry that follows a divided heart.
Week 7: Session 5, The Narrow Gate, judging, asking, and the two ways, with Bonhoeffer on cheap and costly grace.
Week 8: Session 6, The House on the Rock, hearing and doing and the storm that reveals the foundation.
Week 9: Integration. Revisit all six practices, the scripture index, and the one thing each person most needs to do, with space to act on it.

glossary.definition: The opening blessings of the sermon (Matthew 5:3-12), naming the citizens of the kingdom: the poor in spirit, the mourning, the meek and the rest. They describe a life surrendered to the King, not a ladder of virtues.
The first beatitude and the door into the whole sermon: admitting that you have nothing to bring to God. It's the only qualification for a kingdom that is given, not earned.
This study's name for the order Jesus announces, in which the world's reckoning is reversed: the meek inherit the earth and the empty-handed are blessed.
Jesus taking the law from the outward act to the heart beneath it, naming anger as the root of murder and the lustful look as adultery in the heart (Matthew 5:21-30).
Jesus' images for his people in Matthew 5:13-16. Both exist for what surrounds them and stop being themselves when turned inward.

The command in Matthew 5:43-48 to refuse personal revenge and seek the good of those who hate you, grounded in the Father who sends rain on the just and the unjust. It never requires staying in danger.
What Jesus commends in Matthew 6:19-21, against treasure on earth that perishes. The heart follows the treasure, so what we invest in shapes what we love.
Jesus' statement that no one can serve God and money (Matthew 6:24). Money becomes a master when it's trusted to keep us safe, prove our worth or guarantee tomorrow.
The image in Matthew 7:13-14 of the hard way that leads to life, against the wide and easy road that leads to destruction.
The closing parable of the sermon (Matthew 7:24-27): two builders whose houses look the same until the storm, divided not by hearing the words but by doing them.
Bonhoeffer's term, from The Cost of Discipleship, for grace that forgives without changing anyone: "grace without discipleship, grace without the cross."

Bonhoeffer's term for the grace of the narrow gate: costly because it costs a person his life, grace because it gives him the only true life. He compares it to the treasure hidden in a field (Matthew 13:44).
Jesus' picture in Matthew 7:3-5 of someone inspecting the speck in another's eye with a log in his own. Take out the log first, so you can see clearly enough to help.

promoKit.inviteCaption: Jesus began his most famous sermon by blessing people the world had written off, and ended it with a storm. A six-session study on the Sermon on the Mount: the Beatitudes, the deeper law, loving enemies, treasure and worry, the narrow gate, and the house that holds.
quoteCards: The only qualification for the kingdom is admitting you have none. Blessed are the poor in spirit.
Jesus didn't lower the law. He took it past the hand to the heart, where we actually live.
We love our enemies because we were the enemies, and were loved first.
Money becomes a god the moment you ask it to do what only God can do.
Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. The treasure goes first, and the heart follows.
The wide gate is crowded because it lets you carry everything through.
The storm comes to both houses. It doesn't decide whether you stand. It shows what you were standing on.
Don't only admire this sermon. Do it.
